## The supported explanation

The completed controls identify coherent numerical age assignment and head–encoder coadaptation as useful parts of the learning rule in this ImageNet fine-tuning regime. Scalar point learning supplies a persistent numerical task: it predicts one age statistic through a shared score and corrects errors in that statistic. A structured categorical starting function can supply useful numerical organization while retaining a full classifier. The readout, loss weights, available flexibility and useful training horizon determine the resulting held-out point prediction. These controls establish numerical-structure and update effects; MAE's removal of residual-magnitude weighting supplies a further property motivating its use for a point decision.

This hypothesis has a concrete intervention behind it. We changed the numerical age assignment of a full categorical head while preserving its base binomial coefficients, initial probability multiset, entropy, head norm, rank and attainable family. The coherent assignment improved selected test MAE by **0.733 years clean** and **1.183 years under SD-10**, with every paired block agreeing. The gain also survived fitting a common readout to the resulting encoders. Numerical assignment therefore contributes beyond the preserved properties in this training regime.

These are three paired joint blocks on one reused split. The conclusion concerns the registered training and readout procedures; individual block results accompany every main comparison.

The objectives supply numerical structure in different ways. Point losses directly organize fitting around an age mean or median. TailRL uses overlapping numerical age-radius windows and fits their probabilities. Categorical CE fits label probabilities; ordered binomial initialization gives its initial encoder correction an age-mean residual. Both the loss definition and the starting function can therefore supply a numerical task for feature learning.

### What numerical sharing gives the encoder

Let $h$ be the pooled image representation and $s=w^\top h+b$ a shared score. A binomial starting function has

$$
z_a=\log {99\choose a}+as,\qquad \mu_F=99\operatorname{sigmoid}(s).
$$

Its per-example CE correction to the image features is exactly

$$
\nabla_h L_F=w(\mu_F-y).
$$

The encoder receives a numerical age residual along one learned feature direction. Conditional expectation gives $w[\mu_F-\mathbb E(Y\mid h)]$. A scalar mean head maintains this kind of numerical correction throughout learning, with its loss supplying the residual weight. Scalar MAE instead supplies a median-directed sign correction.

In the symmetric-swap control, an involution $\pi$ exchanges 25 of the 50 age pairs $\{a,99-a\}$. Binomial symmetry preserves each age's base coefficient, but the initial correction becomes

$$
\nabla_h L_P=w[\mu_F-\pi(y)],
\qquad
\mathbb E[\nabla_h L_P\mid h]
=w\{\mu_F-\mathbb E[\pi(Y)\mid h]\}.
$$

The shared direction now receives the numerical residual of the altered age code. Both fields are one dimensional. Their distinction is the meaning assigned to the target in that field.

A working-score calculation makes this distinction explicit. A one-score CE family averages its label code. Universal recovery of the physical-age mean from that single coded mean characterizes nonconstant affine age codes, including global reversal with an opposite score convention. The saved partial swaps admit designed label laws with the same coded mean and different physical-age means. At the centered state their expected coded correction cancels while the ordered correction retains the age-mean residual. The ordinary full head retains a repair gradient; this calculation describes the initial encoder channel within the complete training intervention.

At the centered score $s=0$, the two heads give identical probabilities, target CE and individual feature-gradient magnitudes. The selected symmetric pairs reverse correction sign. This gives a precise local illustration of how numerical assignment organizes the encoder's learning signal. The actual image experiment evaluates the full assignment change at varying scores, with shared minibatches, encoder Jacobians, clipping and Adam.

Ordered assignment links correction sign to physical age; each swapped symmetric pair reverses it while preserving the individual magnitude at this anchor. The plots enumerate possible target ages.](evidence/age-assignment/centered-age-corrections.png){#fig-centered-assignment width=100%}

### The gain transfers to a full categorical learner

An ordinary float32 categorical CE head with ordered binomial initialization reaches clean selected MAE **5.398**, compared with **6.050** for the same architecture under ordinary random initialization. The three paired gains are **0.755, 0.704 and 0.499 years**. Every categorical output remains available during training.

Keeping an additional scalar-score path produces clean selected MAE **5.448**. Its endpoint difference from the ordinary ordered head varies in sign, while its early trajectory changes substantially. Parameter coordinates affect the path even when the starting policies coincide. The ordinary ordered head already obtains the large clean initialization benefit.

The common-readout experiment locates a representation contribution. At epoch 50, the same supplied-label ridge procedure gives ordered-minus-random CE differences **−1.668, −1.688 and −1.697 years**. Under SD-10, the average gains are **0.747 years** with supplied-label ridge and **1.128 years** with the clean-label diagnostic. These are changes in age accessibility under a specified readout procedure.

The stronger assignment control preserves the base shape and low-rank structure of the ordered starting function. Ordered-minus-swapped differences are:

| Outcome | Clean labels | Fixed SD-10 |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Validation-selected native test MAE | −0.733 | −1.183 |
| Epoch-50 native test MAE | −0.881 | −1.102 |
| Epoch-50 supplied-label ridge test MAE | −1.098 | −0.849 |
| Epoch-50 oracle-clean ridge test MAE | −1.098 | −0.788 |

All underlying block comparisons favor the ordered assignment, including the epoch-25 common probes. The swapped start has better aggregate initial validation MAE and NLL, so the observed advantage develops during learning. The swapped package retains some improvements over ordinary random initialization, consistent with useful structure remaining in its symmetric base prior and folded age information.

The identified intervention is numerical assignment under the declared update rule. Its consequences include target-dependent correction signs, relative weights, probabilities and clipping. The centered identity explains an available local mechanism; the training comparison measures the complete intervention.

### Scalar sharing and flexible point prediction have a tradeoff

A shared age score supplies a strong organization for feature learning. A categorical mean can also provide a useful nonlinear readout of the same features. In the first 50-epoch cohort, categorical mean-MSE has lower selected MAE than scalar MSE in all three clean and all three noisy blocks, averaging advantages of **0.203** and **0.149 years**. Conversely, the epoch-50 clean scalar-MSE features give better common-ridge prediction by **0.209 years** on average. The stored readout and linear feature accessibility measure different properties.

Frozen ImageNet features give a useful boundary for the fitted readout recipes: the retained scalar-MAE head has MAE **9.086**, while TailRL reaches **7.871**. The richer categorical mapping, objective and finite optimization all form this comparison. End-to-end adaptation gives the encoder an additional way to organize its features around a numerical age score.

The within-score loss comparison further identifies the role of weights. Scalar MSE and binomial CE use the same sigmoid mean family and score initialization. Clean binomial CE improves selected MAE by **0.338 years** and final common-ridge MAE by **0.506 years**. Their scalar derivatives are

$$
\partial_s L_{\mathrm{BinCE}}=\mu-y,\qquad
\partial_s L_{\mathrm{MSE}}=\frac{2(\mu-y)q(1-q)}{99},\qquad
\partial_s L_{\mathrm{MAE}}=\operatorname{sign}(\mu-y)q(1-q).
$$

These weights change the minibatch correction and the optimizer's response. The quasi-score derivation gives a precise variance-dependent comparison in a correctly specified fixed-dimensional mean model: CE weighting is asymptotically optimal within the regular mean estimating equations for the two designed binomial/endpoint laws. Squared-error weighting attains that bound under constant conditional variance. The image results measure the complete learned-representation training rule.

### Regularization controls the cost of additional categorical fitting

The free-versus-affine residual intervention starts from the same function with matched registered parameters. The affine projection retains the shared-score mean class and a redundant location-update path. The free residual adds non-affine categorical directions, changing both mean flexibility and distributional flexibility.

The comparison changes the available directions and the gradients presented to Adam. It identifies that constraint/update intervention under the declared training procedure.

For CE, the free residual has higher selected error than the affine control in every block under both label regimes. At epoch 50, the corresponding common-ridge costs average **0.561 years clean**, **0.312 years with noisy supplied-label ridge** and **0.443 years with the noisy oracle diagnostic**. For TailRL under SD-10, the final common-readout costs are **0.302** and **0.466 years**, again with all block signs agreeing. The clean TailRL comparisons have a different ordering: the benefit of retaining the affine structure depends on the objective and label regime.

The certified synthetic experiment isolates an estimation component with fixed features and a known realizable mean. Under binomial labels, weak residual regularization adds mean-MSE costs of **13.334, 3.065 and 0.521 years²** at training sizes **128, 512 and 2,048**. Strong residual shrinkage approaches the shared-score result. All fitted problems satisfy explicit convex convergence certificates, and a separate NumPy/SciPy implementation reproduces all 180 retained fits' objectives, gradients, predictions and validation choices.

An independent challenger then gives the scalar score its own three-candidate regularization search. Under the high-variance endpoint law at $n=128$, conditional-mean MSE is **212.15** for the original fixed scalar ridge, **206.45** for the selected full estimator and **136.08** for the selected scalar ridge. The latter improves excess mean risk by **34.08%** relative to the selected full procedure, or total observed-label squared risk by **3.04%** after including irreducible noise. This is a useful scalar regularization competitor within the declared candidate sets. Full models can also approach scalar solutions under suitable regularization.

### The fitted readout and encoder coadapt

The head objective changes the gradient field through which the encoder learns, and the encoder changes the features on which the head fits. The routing factorial measures this joint process. Its interactions persist after replacing the final head with a common ridge procedure.

For example, under clean labels at epoch 50, changing the source encoder route from MSE to TailRL improves common-ridge MAE by **0.184 years** when the source head uses MSE, and raises error by **0.358 years** when the source head uses TailRL. Both simple-effect signs repeat across all three blocks. The useful supervision rule depends on its coadapted head.

The late noisy free-Tail case separates native-readout deterioration from continued accessible learning:

| Method and readout | Epoch 25 MAE | Epoch 50 MAE |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Free TailRL, native | 7.411 | 7.967 |
| Free TailRL, supplied-label ridge | 7.452 | 7.389 |
| Free TailRL, oracle-clean ridge | 6.815 | 6.851 |
| Affine TailRL, supplied-label ridge | 7.377 | 7.087 |
| Affine TailRL, oracle-clean ridge | 6.651 | 6.385 |

The free head's native prediction worsens in every block while its common-readout changes are small and mixed. The affine model continues improving under both probes. Thus the observed late gap combines an unfavorable native readout with a relative difference in continued accessible learning. Head replacement changes the fitted procedure, so these observations describe interventions rather than an additive percentage decomposition.

The own-field audit supplies a further distinction. Final within-age corruption-following slopes average **0.939 for free TailRL** and **0.949 for affine TailRL**, while supplied training MAEs are **3.298** and **3.278**. Field following and held-out point accuracy have different orderings here. Free TailRL's decreasing policy variance and entropy identify a distribution-shape trajectory accompanying its native deterioration. A concentration-specific causal claim would require its own intervention.

### Why the scalar-MAE advantage is concentrated in particular regimes

Scalar MAE combines a shared numerical score with a sign-weighted point objective that elicits a conditional median of the supplied-label law. Its residual coefficient is independent of error magnitude. These are exact properties of the recipe. The completed controls establish related numerical-structure and update effects; the historical scalar-MAE advantage supplies the temporal prediction tested by the repeated 500-epoch cohort from random initialization.

The theoretical targets also clarify the comparison. Scalar MSE, categorical CE and the exact unrestricted equal-radius population TailRL objective all recover the conditional mean under their respective realizability conditions. For fresh symmetric noise around a deterministic integer reference age, rounding and clipping retain that age as a supplied-label median, while moving the corrupted-label mean inward near the boundaries. A single fixed noisy label can still be fitted. This target property motivates MAE for the stated label law; the image interventions directly establish the contributions of numerical assignment and the implemented learning rule.

The resulting prediction is conditional and constructive: numerical sharing is useful when the encoder can learn an age representation that supports the chosen point statistic; sufficient readout flexibility helps when that mapping is harder; appropriate weighting, regularization and training horizon keep the learned structure useful. The controlled initialization, constraint, common-readout and synthetic interventions identify these contributions directly. The long-horizon replication supplies the remaining temporal comparison.
